standard.title: Beliefs, values and practices
standard.description: key beliefs, values and practices of an ancient society, with a particular emphasis on one of the following areas: everyday life, warfare, or death and funerary customs
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can describe the organisation and roles of key groups in the ancient society, including how groups influenced and changed society (AC9HH7K10). They have not yet examined the beliefs, values, and practices that shaped how the society understood the world and organised cultural life — the religious, ideological, and practical dimensions of daily existence.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students describe the key beliefs, values, and practices of the ancient society with particular emphasis on one focus area (everyday life, warfare, or death and funerary customs), explain how these beliefs and values shaped the society's practices, and use evidence from sources to support their descriptions.

nodes.label: Religious and cosmological beliefs
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the key religious and cosmological beliefs of the ancient society — including its deities, creation stories, or understanding of the afterlife — and explain how these beliefs shaped the society's values and practices.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least two key religious or cosmological beliefs of the ancient society and explain how each belief shaped a specific practice or institution.
nodes.typical_width: Describe the religious and cosmological beliefs of the ancient society — including its pantheon or deity system, creation narratives, and understanding of the afterlife — and explain how these beliefs shaped social structures, political authority, cultural practices, and the built environment (temples, tombs, monuments).
wider: Examine how religious authority was organised in the ancient society — who had religious power, how it related to political power, and what institutions (priesthoods, temples, oracles) mediated between the human and divine.

Investigate how the society's religious beliefs shaped its understanding of natural events — floods, eclipses, military outcomes — and how this cosmology informed political and social decision-making.

Compare the religious beliefs of the chosen ancient society with those of another ancient society, identifying shared patterns (e.g. polytheism, divine kingship, afterlife beliefs) and significant differences.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat religious beliefs as exotic details rather than coherent systems generating social practices cannot connect N2's focus area practices to the beliefs and values that shaped them — the practices become disconnected from their explanatory context, producing description without understanding.

response_modes.reason: Students at Year 7 often encounter ancient religious beliefs as exotic details rather than as coherent systems that shaped every dimension of social life. The reasoning scaffold — how a belief about divine authority justifies political hierarchy; how a belief in an afterlife drives funerary practice; how cosmological beliefs shape responses to natural events — needs to be made explicit to move students from cataloguing beliefs to understanding their social function.

success_criteria: Describes at least two religious or cosmological beliefs of the ancient society.
Explains how each belief shaped at least one specific practice, institution, or social arrangement.
Does not treat religious beliefs as simply 'superstition' — recognises them as coherent meaning-making systems that shaped social life.

nodes.label: Focus area — everyday life, warfare, or death and funerary customs
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the specific beliefs, values, and practices of the ancient society in their chosen focus area (everyday life, warfare, or death and funerary customs), using evidence from sources to support their account.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least three specific practices in the chosen focus area and connect each to a belief or value that shaped it.
nodes.typical_width: Describe the key practices of the chosen focus area in detail — drawing on multiple types of evidence (artefacts, written sources, visual sources) — and explain how the society's beliefs and values shaped those practices. For everyday life: food, housing, family structures, work, recreation. For warfare: motivations, tactics, weapons, treatment of enemies, warrior culture. For death and funerary customs: burial practices, beliefs about the afterlife, tomb construction, treatment of the dead.
wider: Examine how practices in the focus area varied across different social groups within the society — how did elite and non-elite everyday life differ? How did warfare affect soldiers differently from rulers? How did funerary customs differ by social status?

Investigate specific artefacts or sites associated with the focus area in detail — a specific battle account, a tomb complex, an architectural representation of daily life — and examine what they reveal that general descriptions cannot.

Explore how practices in the focus area changed over time within the ancient society — identifying what was stable (continuity) and what shifted in response to political, environmental, or social changes.

response_modes.reason: The choice of focus area within this descriptor means students can explore one area in depth — but breadth within that area (across social groups, across evidence types, across time periods within the society) is what produces genuine understanding rather than a flat description. Without breadth across these dimensions, students produce a generalised account that misses the differentiation, change, and complexity that makes the area historically interesting.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The focus area approach creates genuine richness — each of everyday life, warfare, and funerary customs opens onto significant archaeological and textual evidence and raises substantive historical questions. Advancing students can examine how the focus area connects to broader beliefs and values, how evidence types reveal different aspects of the same practices, and how change over time within the focus area reflects larger social changes. The variety within each focus area is also inherently broad.
success_criteria: Describes at least three specific practices in the chosen focus area with reference to evidence.
Connects at least two practices to beliefs or values that shaped them — not just describes what people did but why.
Uses at least two types of evidence (artefact, written source, visual source) to support the description.

nodes.label: Beliefs, values, and practices as a window on the society
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how the beliefs, values, and practices of the ancient society — including their chosen focus area — reveal what the society valued, how it organised itself, and what distinguished it from other ancient societies.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how at least two beliefs or values revealed in the focus area reflect the society's broader priorities or worldview.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how the beliefs, values, and practices examined across Nodes 1 and 2 together reveal what the ancient society valued, how it understood itself and the world, and how these beliefs and values shaped its organisation. Identify at least one way in which this society's beliefs or practices were distinctive — different from other ancient societies or from modern perspectives.
wider: Examine how beliefs and values evident in the focus area connect to the society's social structure (K10) and its environmental context (K09) — developing an integrated account of how the society's physical and social worlds reflected and shaped its beliefs.

Investigate how the society's beliefs and practices were represented and interpreted differently by different groups within it — what the elite record says vs what archaeological evidence from non-elite contexts reveals.

Explore how historians and archaeologists have interpreted and reinterpreted the society's beliefs and practices as new evidence has emerged — examining how historical interpretations of ancient belief systems can change.

response_modes.reason: This node integrates religious beliefs (Node 1) and focus area practices (Node 2) into a synthetic account of what the beliefs, values, and practices reveal about the society as a whole. Students must move from describing specific practices to explaining what they reveal — connecting the particular to the general. This integration move is the descriptor's full demand.

success_criteria: Explains how at least two beliefs or values revealed through the focus area reflect the society's broader worldview.
Identifies at least one distinctive feature of this society's beliefs or practices — something that sets it apart.
Moves beyond description to explanation — not just what the society did, but what it reveals about what they valued.
